title: Longest Continuous Increasing Subsequence
description: Brute force to optimized: walking forward from every start versus a single Kadane's-style running streak counter.

blocks.text: Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest CONTINUOUS (contiguous) increasing subsequence: a run of consecutive elements where each is strictly greater than the one before it.

blocks.caption: Extend a running streak while strictly increasing; reset to 1 the moment it breaks

blocks.text: Given an array nums, find the length of the longest stretch of consecutive elements where each one is strictly larger than the element right before it.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting the Longest Unbroken Climb
blocks.text: Like hiking along a trail and tracking the longest unbroken uphill climb, where "unbroken" means every single step must go strictly higher than the step before it. The moment a step goes flat or downhill, the current climb streak ends completely, and a brand new streak of length 1 begins from that point.

blocks.caption: Every element either continues the current climb or breaks it, resetting the streak

blocks.text: Before checking every possible starting position and walking forward from each one, notice that the streak length at any position only ever depends on the position right before it.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The length of the increasing streak ending at position i is either (the streak ending at i-1) + 1, if nums[i] > nums[i-1], or exactly 1, if it isn't.

Observation 2: This mirrors Kadane's Algorithm's "extend or restart" recurrence exactly, just applied to a streak LENGTH instead of a running SUM.

Observation 3: A single running variable, current, can track this streak length, updated in O(1) at each position based only on comparing the current and previous elements.

Observation 4: Track the maximum value of current seen across the whole pass.

Recognizing this as "Kadane's Algorithm, but for streak length instead of sum" immediately suggests the same single-pass, O(1)-per-element technique.

This is a direct structural cousin of Kadane's Algorithm: instead of tracking a running sum that resets when it goes negative, track a running streak length that resets to 1 whenever the increasing condition breaks.
For every possible starting index, extend forward as long as the sequence keeps strictly increasing.

items: For every possible starting index, walk forward while each next element is strictly greater than the previous one.
Track the length of the longest such walk found across every starting position.

codes.python:
def find_length_of_lcis(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    best = 1
    for start in range(n):
        length = 1
        end = start
        while end + 1 < n and nums[end + 1] > nums[end]:                     # keep extending while strictly increasing
            end += 1
            length += 1
        best = max(best, length)
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(find_length_of_lcis([1, 3, 5, 4, 7]))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every starting index is tried explicitly, since this brute force does not yet share work between overlapping streaks.
The inner walk stops the moment the strictly-increasing condition fails, since continuing further from this same start could never help.
best only ever increases, tracking the single longest streak found across every starting position.

blocks.text: Every possible starting position is checked directly, walking forward while strictly increasing, so the correct maximum is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) in the worst case, since each of the n starting positions can walk forward up to n elements.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: restarting the walk from scratch at every new starting position ignores that the streak length at any position depends only on the position immediately before it, exactly like Kadane's Algorithm.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force re-walks from every starting position independently. Instead, maintain a single running streak length: at each position, either extend it by 1 (if the current element is strictly greater than the previous one) or reset it to 1 (otherwise). Track the maximum streak length seen throughout this single linear pass.

Maintain current, the length of the increasing streak ending at the current position, and best, the longest streak seen anywhere so far. At each position (from the second element onward), update current based on whether nums[i] > nums[i-1], then update best.
Track a single running streak length, resetting it to 1 whenever the strictly-increasing condition breaks.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with O(1) work per element.
Space: O(1) extra.

current always represents the length of the increasing streak ending exactly at the current position. Since a streak either continues from the position right before it (if strictly increasing) or must restart entirely (if not), the recurrence needs no information from any position further back than the immediately preceding one, exactly mirroring why Kadane's Algorithm's running sum only depends on the previous position.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["nums[i] > nums[i-1]","Extend the current streak by 1"],["nums[i] <= nums[i-1]","Reset the current streak to length 1, starting fresh at position i"]]}

items: current and best are both initialized to 1, since a single element is trivially an increasing streak of length 1.
The comparison nums[i] > nums[i-1] uses strict inequality, correctly treating equal consecutive elements as breaking the streak.
best is updated every iteration, since the longest streak could end at any position, not just the last one.

blocks.text: This problem is structurally identical to Kadane's Algorithm, just tracking a streak LENGTH that resets to 1 on a broken condition, instead of a running SUM that resets to the current element on a negative running total.

items: Using a non-strict comparison (>=) instead of strict (>), which would incorrectly extend the streak across equal consecutive elements.
Resetting current to 0 instead of 1 when the streak breaks, which would undercount the length of the fresh streak starting at the current position.

Confusing this with the general (non-contiguous) Longest Increasing Subsequence problem, which requires a substantially more complex DP or binary-search-based solution; this "continuous" version needs neither.

items: Explicitly name the connection to Kadane's Algorithm ("same extend-or-reset recurrence, just for streak length instead of sum"), since recognizing this structural similarity demonstrates strong pattern transfer rather than treating this as an unrelated new problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Longest run of CONSECUTIVE elements satisfying a simple pairwise condition" points toward a single running streak counter, reset whenever the condition breaks, mirroring Kadane's Algorithm's structure exactly.

items: How would you also report the actual streak (start and end indices)? Track a tentative start index, resetting it whenever the streak breaks, and record the (start, end) pair whenever best is updated.

How does this differ from the general Longest Increasing Subsequence problem? That problem allows the subsequence to skip elements (non-contiguous), requiring O(n log n) DP with binary search; this "continuous" version only ever looks at strictly consecutive array elements, needing just a single linear pass.
What if the condition were "non-decreasing" instead of "strictly increasing"? Simply change the comparison from > to >=, and the same running-streak technique still applies unchanged.

A direct structural cousin of Kadane's Algorithm (Maximum Subarray), applying the same "extend or reset based only on the immediately preceding state" recurrence to a streak length instead of a running sum.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (Kadane's-style running streak): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Kadane's-style running streak counter, resetting to 1 whenever the strictly-increasing condition breaks
Core Idea: The streak ending at any position either extends the streak from the position before it, or restarts fresh, depending only on that one prior comparison
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: This is structurally identical to Kadane's Algorithm, just tracking a streak length instead of a running sum
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: current = nums[i] > nums[i-1] ? current + 1 : 1; best = max(best, current)
